title: The Time Horizon Problem
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that most organizational tension, burnout and churn come from a mismatch between the goals leaders announce and the time horizon their structures actually support. She contrasts the short-term workplace, driven by quick wins, quarterly incentives and short leader tenures, with the long-term workplace that invests in learning, trust and leadership continuity. Her central move is to reframe the so-called leadership pipeline problem as a design problem rather than a failure of individuals. She explains why short-termism persists, citing board and investor pressure, annual performance reviews and the glamour of new initiatives over culture work. The piece closes with five concrete practices, including naming and protecting a time horizon, changing what is measured, designing leadership transitions for continuity, building in reflection, and ring-fencing capability-building budgets. It is a substantive structural argument, though the Deloitte and tenure statistics are cited without sources.
points: Most organizations have goals but are dishonest about time: the horizon their incentives and systems support often contradicts what leaders say they want.
The leadership pipeline problem is reframed as a design problem, since short-tenure, high-pressure roles cycle leaders through systems that do not give them time or support to succeed.
Short-termism is reinforced structurally through quarterly executive pay, 12-18 month board windows and annual reviews that only measure what is easy to assess.
Long-term workplaces build learning infrastructure, trust and leadership continuity, which often makes them more adaptable in the long run.
Practical moves include committing to an explicit evaluation horizon such as 18 months, tracking leading indicators of capability, and overlapping outgoing and incoming leaders.
quotes: Every organization has goals, but few organizations are honest about time. More specifically, I’d argue that they fail to recognize the time horizon the systems, incentives, and leadership expectations surrounding their goals function within, and ultimately, how that supports their ability to achieve said goals.

And through that experience—which I made the conscious choice to remove myself from—I learned that this pipeline problem that everyone keeps talking about? It’s actually not really a pipeline problem—it’s a design problem.
Many organizations tie executive compensation to annual or quarterly goals, not multi-year outcomes. Boards often operate on twelve to eighteen month evaluation windows.

Many of us have also seen organizations celebrate “speed” and “rapid iteration” while penalizing those behind the scenes saying, “We’re not ready yet,” or, “We need another few months before we can fully assess this.” In organizations with short-term orientations, the language of agility is often weaponized against that of patience.

Over time, the organization becomes very good at starting lots of things and very bad at finishing the ones that really get the whole ship moving forward. There's constant motion in the form of new initiatives, new tools, and new priorities, but none of it compounds, because it’s neither connected nor built out enough to stick.

When leaders know they’ll be around long enough to live with the consequences of their decisions, they’re likely to make different choices. To invest in foundational work like clarifying roles, building processes and systems, and developing people, because they know there’s a lot to be gained long-term. While short-term leadership incentivizes shortcuts, long-term leadership incentivizes infrastructure.

If everything that gets rewarded shows up in quarters, but everything that matters takes years, you’ve got a serious structural mismatch. Start bringing attention to leading indicators that point toward long-term capability—things like time-to-competence for new hires, decision quality over time, reduction in escalations, improvement in engagement scores over a year.
